statement: Solomana Kanté (Souleymane Kanté) created N'Ko in Guinea/Côte d'Ivoire, completed 1949, after experimenting with and rejecting adaptations of Arabic and Latin script for Maninka's tone and vowel system. N'Ko is genuinely alphabetic (19 consonants, 7 vowels, 8 diacritics), written right-to-left and visually resembling Arabic script, but structurally diverges from it with obligatory tone marking — a stimulus-diffusion signature (visual/directional influence from Arabic, phonemic/tonal system built from scratch). The oft-repeated motivating anecdote — that Kanté was responding to a Lebanese journalist (attributed to Kamel Mrowa, founder of the Beirut daily Al-Hayat, 1946) claiming African languages were "unwritable" — is well-attested as N'Ko community/institutional history but was not independently confirmed to a source outside that tradition this session; Kanté's biographical background in Arabic and Ajami manuscript scholarship is independently documented regardless of the anecdote's precise accuracy.
